my new take tbqh is that if any line of code is over 90 days old at the company we are doing it wrong. 


greenfield projects should never be left to just grow without rewrites. the cruft and awfulness of a vibed codebase after months of work is disgusting honestly
brownfield projects have a large number of footguns, bugs, and performance problems that agents will trivially fix
the theory that “agents can write bad code because future agents will maintain it” is outright incorrect. awful take. instead, future agents will simply rewrite it and make it more sane
if you cannot rewrite a project without worrying about it, you don’t have enough test coverage, and that is bad anyway 


i genuinely do believe we need to pick this thinking up. we are maintaining and spending so much of our time on just maintenance and dealing with problems we shouldn't have anymore. we are not prepared for scaling at the rates we may soon need to, and every day that we get ahead of these problems counts.

The problem was entirely that the code was written for a compiler, not a reader.

- Naming: probe.ts held the sandbox check while toolchain.ts held the probe. inputs.ts was a grab-bag of path validation, file I/O, hashing, JSON parsing, and the error type.
- Density: comma-chained declarations, bare offsets like data.readUInt32LE(at + 20) and & 0x2002, and calls like check(name, status, detail, true, {...}) where you had to know the parameter order to read them.
- No "why" anywhere: there were no module comments, and non-obvious choices had no explanation. Examples include why /nologo is filtered out, what the supervisor script waits for, and why __proto__ keys get restored. Each of those took me a minute to work out.
- Giant closures: toolchainProbe was a 230-line function mutating a shared report. The sandbox runner was one closure with eight mutable lets.
- Copy-paste instead of helpers: open/hash/close try-finally appeared about ten times, the read loop four times, and the quarantine handling twice.
- Defensive noise: typeof x !== "string" on parameters typed string, and a typeof check on a config value that had already been validated. Your CLAUDE.md asks it not to do that.
- Dead or vestigial bits:
  - a required parameter that no caller passed;
  - an unused stopChild variable;
  - schemas exported but never imported;
  - the tool-to-variable mapping kept in two places (the schema derived it from the tool name, while toolInventory.ts had its own table).
- The test pattern: test.each(Object.entries({ async "name"(root) {...} }))("%s", ...) is the clearest sign of it optimising for something other than readability. It saved a line of setup per test, and every test became harder to find and read.

My overall read: it reasons well about failure modes and adversarial input, but it doesn't model the next person reading the code. It optimises for few lines and for having checked every case, not for being understood. Its taste was the problem, not its judgement.

· Thought · 6.8s

P17 finding documented: FastCGI SetHandler canonical SCRIPT_FILENAME RCE.

At HEAD b0f6b8d5, fastcgi::handler target for file still builds the wire SCRIPT_FILENAME from actual_path (the canonical symlink target), even though Target.script_filename is documented as the lexical request-mapped value and P15 fixed the ProxyPassMatch/PATH_INFO constructor. PHP-FPM therefore applies security.limit_extensions to a different name than Apache.

Observed chain - global/per-directory SetHandler, uploads hardened with SetHandler none, and an in-root symlink:

/uploads/shell.php          -> static source on both servers
/pub/upload-link.txt -> ../uploads/shell.php

· Apache: 403 Access denied. - FPM sees pub/upload-link.txt (.txt)
· vapahe: 200 PHPEXEC uploads-shell uid=33 - FPM sees uploads/shell.php (.php)

The FPM access log confirms the drift (Apache lexical vs vapahe canonical). Case C demonstrates the same result through an access-file proxy handler; case D shows canonical <Location>/<Directory> denials still bind, so this is a backend policy-gate bypass, not an auth-guard bypass.

Files added/updated

· adversarial/findings_p17.md - root cause, exploit chain, evidence, impact, fix, scope.
· adversarial/p17/exploit_p17.py - 15-verdict differential harness (cases A-D), rerun successfully: 15 verdict(s) passed.
· adversarial/README.md - P17 index entry and reproduction section.

No product source was modified. The benchmark ProxyPassMatch branch remains fixed by P15; P17 affects the documented SetHandler deployment class when the handler scope covers the lexical non-PHP name (global/per-directory or access-file handler).

The Threshold at Ashdod
The priests of Ashdod came into the temple one morning, sometime in the eleventh century before our era if we take the Book of Samuel at its word, and found their god face down on the floor before the captured Ark of the Covenant. They set him upright. The next morning he had fallen again, and this time his head and both palms lay severed on the threshold, and only the trunk remained. The text adds that the priests of Dagon, to this day, do not tread on that threshold. They step over it.
That severed god is the root of everything Lovecraft does with his Deep Ones, though the root is stranger than the plant. Dagan, as the Bronze Age tablets of Ebla, Mari, and Ugarit show, was a Levantine god of grain and storm, with no fish in him at
